narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the third decile, noticeably lower than the average of accepted students who typically rank around the sixth decile. This lower standing signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.50 it is higher than the 3.23 average among accepted students, so this factor pulled the prediction toward passing and helped offset some of the risk. However, it was not enough to overcome the other influences.

Your LSAT score of 33 was the third most important factor and increased the chance of failure. It sits below the 37.18 average of students who were admitted, indicating the model saw room for improvement in test performance.

Taken together, these academic signals led the system to conclude your overall profile carried too high a risk of bar failure. To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your class rank if you continue law school, or consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score. Improving either area would likely shift the model’s assessment in your favor. (248 words)
